title: Mastery Challenge: Literature
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Literature Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Ten questions from across the tree: epics and myths, the flood tablet, Ovid, fairy tales, detectives, dystopias, Tolkien and translation.

cards.headline: The Literature Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from clay tablets to Middle-earth. Level 1 asked how literature got from spoken stories to the novel on your shelf. Now see how far you've traveled. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Literature: mastered
learned: How stories traveled from voices and clay tablets to epics, novels and fairy tales on the page.
Why the same story, from Cinderella to the Odyssey, changes with each teller and translator.
How detective stories, science fiction and dystopias each set their own rules for readers.
What makes a classic worth reading, and how to place one in its tradition.

questions.prompt: Which of these describes an epic rather than a novel?

options.label: An invented prose story about imperfect people
A short animal tale with a moral
A long narrative poem about heroic deeds
A set of rules for playing fair with clues

questions.explanation: An epic is a long narrative poem recounting heroic deeds, like Gilgamesh or Homer's poems.

questions.prompt: Why does this tree never use the word myth to mean "false"?

options.label: Scholars use it for a traditional sacred story
Every myth has since been proved true
options.rationale: Truth isn't what the word is about.

options.label: Myths are only about talking animals
A myth is any story told as history

questions.explanation: In the scholarly sense a myth is a traditional, symbolic story tied to religious belief, not a falsehood.

questions.prompt: In Genesis, the flood answers human wrongdoing. What brings the flood in the Babylonian story?

options.label: A disagreement among the gods
A king's search for a plant of youth
A serpent stealing from the gods
Humans building a tower to heaven

questions.explanation: The Babylonian flood comes from a disagreement among the gods; in Genesis, from human wrongdoing.

questions.prompt: In which creation story does an animal dive into the water and bring up the earth that becomes land?

options.label: Pan Gu and the cosmic egg
Marduk and Tiamat's waters
Sky Woman and the muskrat
Hesiod's Chaos
options.rationale: That's order out of chaos too.

questions.explanation: In the Haudenosaunee story, the muskrat dives for earth, which grows on the turtle's back into Turtle Island.

questions.prompt: Which tale from Ovid is acted by workmen in A Midsummer Night's Dream and helped inspire Romeo and Juliet?

options.label: Daphne and the laurel
options.rationale: Daphne is Ovid's, but not this one.

options.label: Hou Yi and the ten suns
Gilgamesh and Enkidu
Pyramus and Thisbe

questions.explanation: Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe became the workmen's play in A Midsummer Night's Dream and one inspiration for Romeo and Juliet.

questions.prompt: How did Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales differ from the Grimms'?

options.label: He collected his from oral storytellers
He invented almost all of his own
He translated Perrault's into Danish
He only wrote tales with happy endings

questions.explanation: The Grimms took most of their tales from oral sources; all but a dozen of Andersen's 156 tales are his own creations.

questions.prompt: A detective solves the case with a letter that the reader never got to see. What has gone wrong?

options.label: The criminal was mentioned too early
options.rationale: Knox wanted the criminal mentioned early.

options.label: Nothing: detectives may keep secrets
options.rationale: Fair play says they may not.

options.label: It breaks fair play: the reader must see each clue
The story needed a narrating friend
options.rationale: That's a pattern, not the problem here.

questions.explanation: Fair play means clues reach the reader when they reach the detective; Knox: no clue that isn't shown to the reader at once.

questions.prompt: Bilbo takes a cup from a sleeping dragon, as a thief does in Beowulf. How did Tolkien himself explain the likeness?

options.label: Beowulf was a valued source; the theft arose naturally
He never read Beowulf until later
His publisher added the scene
options.rationale: Nothing like that is on the cards.

options.label: He copied it from Ovid's Metamorphoses

questions.explanation: In 1938 Tolkien called Beowulf among his most valued sources, but said the theft arose naturally from his story.

questions.prompt: Which pairing matches Postman's contrast between Nineteen Eighty-Four and Brave New World?

options.label: Orwell: control by pleasure; Huxley: by fear
Both: control by secret police
Orwell: control by fear; Huxley: by pleasure
Both: perfect societies worth copying

questions.explanation: Orwell's Party rules by surveillance and fear; Huxley's World State keeps people content with soma. What we hate, and what we love.

questions.prompt: Why does this tree name the translator, such as Samuel Butler, whenever it quotes Homer?

options.label: Each translation reflects one translator's choices
Homer wrote in English, so only spelling differs
All translations use the same words
options.rationale: Butler and Pope differ even on one sunrise.

options.label: Translators wrote the Odyssey themselves

questions.explanation: Butler's prose keeps the repeated formulas; Pope's couplets vary them. Every translation is someone's set of choices.
